en: The Pratijñāsūtra. Homage to the venerable Veda-Puruṣa. Now follows the Pratijñā: The designation "Veda" applies to both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. In that pure Yājuṣa recension belonging to the Mādhyandina school, the rules for accents in the Mantra portion are as follows: the heart is unaccented (anudātta), the head is accented (udātta), and at the root of the ear is the circumflex (svarita). Thus are the *jātya* and other accents described. In the Brāhmaṇa, however, there are the udātta and anudātta, as well as the *bhāṣika* and *svara* accents. The Sūtras have the *tāna* accent and follow the rules of the Chandas (Vedic meters). 1.

Now, regarding the first of the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), when it occurs at the beginning of a word and is joined with another consonant—even if that [other consonant] is joined [with others]—there is no distinction whether it is joined with the letter *r*, a sibilant (*ūṣman*), or the letter *ṛ*; thus, upon pronunciation at the beginning, middle, or end, there is the pronunciation of the letter *j*. This is the same even in the case of doubling (*dvirbhāva*). Then, for the other semi-vowel (*y*), when it is not joined with another consonant, there is pronunciation accompanied by a sibilant, the letter *ṛ*, or the letter *e*. Similarly, for the third semi-vowel (*v*), in some cases; however, for the letter *ṛ* itself, whether joined or unjoined, this is the same everywhere. Finally, for the last of the semi-vowels (*s*)— [The text continues with further phonetic rules.]

Furthermore, the pronunciation of [the letter *ṣ*] occurring at the beginning, middle, or end of a word is threefold—by way of heavy, medium, and light articulation—and likewise for the retroflex (*mūrdhan*) sibilants (*ūṣman*) when uncombined; however, when combined, there is the pronunciation of the letter *kh*, except in the case of *ṭu*. This occurs naturally during the time of recitation and other such activities.

Now, the substitution of *anusvāra* by *m* occurs before the letters *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*, and *r*; its threefold nature has been explained through the distinctions of short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and heavy (*guru*). A short vowel following a long vowel [becomes long], a long vowel following a short vowel [becomes long], and a heavy vowel following a heavy vowel [becomes heavy]. Among the *parasavarṇa* substitutes, [the *anusvāra*] remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*); elsewhere, in the case of *visarga*s, there is a slight pause (*īṣadvirāma*). For an *anusvāra* at the beginning of a word that follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyukta*), both a slight lengthening (*īṣaddīrghatā*) and a slight pause occur. Thus ends the *Pratijñāsūtra* of Kātyāyana’s *Pariśiṣṭa*.
